newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-LEADING PERSONALITIES REJECT TIME-OUTS AND TWO REFEREES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-LEADING PERSONALITIES REJECT TIME-OUTS AND TWO REFEREES.

text.p: Some of the leading personalities in world soccer rejected on Friday the concept of time-outs and two referees and expressed mixed views on the golden goal.
Task Force 2000, a 24-man group including Johan Cruyff, Franz Beckenbauer and Michel Platini set up after the sterile 1990 World Cup, met for three hours on Friday.

Beckenbauer, the only man to captain and manage a World Cup winning team, said afterwards: "We met for three hours and we are not going to change the world of soccer in that time. But a lot of good ideas came out in discussion. We must remember that we should not complicate football, as one of its real qualities is its simplicity. Nevertheless, it's time too, to keep it alive with new ideas."
The golden goal was used to decide this summer's European soccer championship in which Germany beat the Czech Republic 2-1 with Oliver Bierhoff scoring the sudden-death winner.
But opinion was divided on its future. Cruyff was in favour of an American-style shoot-out to decide drawn matches, while Platini said he preferred the golden goal.

"It is based on a positive concept of a goal being scored," he said. Beckenbauer felt the idea should be given another chance, while FIFA president Joao Havelange said he was in favour of penalties deciding matches after 90 minutes.
But FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter said: "Almost everybody was, in principle, against the golden goal idea -- and everyone was against the idea of time-outs."
The idea of introducing time-outs into the game has been mooted by TV executives keen for more advertising time being made available during matches.

Beckenbauer, former German international Hansi Mueller and Havelange himself were strongly opposed to the idea and Blatter said: "Time-outs are not a hot issue for FIFA right now. It is a problem for TV, it is not FIFA's problem, it is TV's problem."

One suggestion which could gain approval was a further refiement of the back-pass rule, introduced two years ago to speed up the game at the back with the goalkeeper no longer able to catch the ball kicked back to him by one of his own team- mates.
Goalkeepers can still hold the ball headed or chested back, but in future the law may be altered so that goalkeepers can again catch the ball kicked back to them but only for four or five seconds.

Platini and former Italian international Roberto Bettega said they were opposed to the idea of the back pass rule being re-drafted to prevent a back pass with any part of the body, while Bettega said there should be experiments forcing the goalkeeper to play the ball back into play more quickly.
There was widespread opposition to the idea of two referees being introduced to officiate at matches.

Former Dutch and AC Milan striker Marco Van Basten had a novel idea which raised some eyebrows that football should adopt the basketball rule that if a player committs five fouls he is sent off but replaced by a substitute.

While all of these points were only for discussion, some of them may be adopted by national associations and put forward as proposals to football's law-making body, the International Board, which meets in Belfast on March 1.
